brand.rationale: Quoda cleared every filter from every specialist without a single disqualifying strike. Two syllables, stress-first (QUO-da), phonetically identical for TR and US speakers, no false cognates, no semantic baggage, semantically adjacent to 'code' without desperation. The Q letterform is the logo — built from QR module geometry, not a typeface character, meaning the brand mark IS the product artifact. Glyph is the runner-up for visual elegance and domain plausibility, but the silent 'ph' creates recall friction on printed stickers and the .com is likely unaffordable. Quoda owns its frequency entirely.
tagline_options: The QR code that never breaks.
Make it once. Trust it always.

philosophy: Every token, every interaction, every pixel earns the word reliable.

resolutions.decision: Quoda wins unanimously. Register quoda.io as canonical domain immediately; pursue quoda.com as redirect. Wordmark: Inter 300 lowercase, tracking -0.02em, never uppercase, never bold, never drop-shadowed. The Q logomark is constructed from QR module squares — the brand mark is literally the product artifact. This alignment between logo geometry and product geometry is a rare and load-bearing brand argument.
resolutions.winning_argument: Kaan's observation that the Q letterform is the logomark — built from the same square modules that compose the QR code — made this more than a naming decision. Every other candidate was eliminated on at least one filter: Glyph leaks .com via the silent 'ph' and is likely unaffordable; Glify is unmemorable and market-noisy; Tagn fails the whisper test. Quoda passes the whisper test, the printed-sticker typeability test, the two-language phonetic test, and the decade-from-now test. Deniz's tiebreaker: recall and typeability from a printed sticker is the correct criterion because that is where word-of-mouth and direct traffic originate.
resolutions.dissent: Mira warned that an invented word requires the brand to do 100% of the meaning-building — there is no semantic gravity to lean on. If the visual system and UX underperform, 'Quoda' names nothing. The name only works if every other decision in this document is executed at the same level of conviction.

resolutions.decision: Calm Apple-style hero whose centerpiece IS a live, visible, immediately usable generator. One large QR code and one URL input field exist in visual balance above the fold, wrapped in generous whitespace. The QR renders in real time as the user types. The input is visible and focusable on load — not hidden behind a click. The CTA is 'Make it permanent' not 'Generate'. No signup wall for static generation. Email captured only at the moment of dynamic QR creation or analytics access. Time-to-first-QR under 3 seconds is the activation North Star metric, measured with keyboard-only and screen reader testing, not mouse only.
resolutions.winning_argument: Deniz demolished Mira's pure-static-QR position with one empirical fact: 70-80% of landing visits are on mobile — users cannot scan their own screen. The scan-as-demo hero fails for the majority of the audience. Mira conceded the path if not the form: 'I concede the hero QR must have a clear and immediate path to making your own code.' The synthesis is not luxury vs conversion — it is luxury AND conversion because a live generator that works perfectly and instantly IS the luxury statement. Selin's accessibility frame is adopted wholesale: the generator is present in the DOM on load, role=form with aria-label, aria-live='polite' on the QR preview region, complete keyboard navigation from input to download in a single Tab sequence.
resolutions.dissent: Mira warned that a visible generator above the fold risks signaling 'free tool' rather than 'product worth paying for.' The guardrail: the CTA must never say 'Generate' — it must say 'Make it permanent' or 'Save forever', appearing only after the user has typed something. The page frame, whitespace proportion, and typographic weight must signal product confidence, not utility. If a user can iframe the generator in 10 minutes, we have demonstrated our commodity feature, not our core value prop.

resolutions.decision: Accent: #0A7EA4 — deep teal-blue, HSL(198, 90%, 34%). Measured contrast ratios: 4.63:1 on #FFFFFF (WCAG AA normal text), 4.19:1 on #0D0D0F (AA large/UI; use accent-hover for normal text on dark). Single token: --color-accent. Used exactly once per viewport on the highest-priority interactive element. QR modules are always dark-on-white regardless of accent color — scannability absolute. No second accent; success, warning, and error states use lightness and opacity shifts of existing tokens.
resolutions.winning_argument: Selin's methodology wins: the accent color must pass WCAG 1.4.3 on both surfaces before any UI ships — measured, not eyeballed. Mira's #5B5BD6 achieves approximately 3.8:1 on #FAFAFA, which fails WCAG AA for normal text and does not ship. Kaan's #0A84FF is Apple system blue — the most recognizable interactive-state color on the planet — which means users evaluate the brand against Apple's own products rather than receiving it as a distinct identity. Deniz's teal direction is correct (calm, prints accurately on signage, not the indigo/purple dev-tool uniform), and Selin's precise measurement of #0A7EA4 produces a verified, ownable, differentiated accent. Teal reads 'precise instrument' on a near-colorless canvas and carries none of the 2021-SaaS-uniform baggage of indigo or the OS-chrome invisibility of system blue.
resolutions.dissent: Kaan warned that teal is Notion-adjacent and that #0A7EA4 is a brand call as much as a contrast call. The guardrail: monitor the teal SaaS landscape annually. If the space becomes saturated (Notion, Atlassian, Linear all converging on this hue band), revisit. The accent color is a CSS token — it can be migrated without a design system rebuild. Mira's instinct that violet-indigo carries 'trust and precision' associations is noted; if #5B5BD6 is ever used, it must only appear on large interactive elements where the lower contrast ratio passes the large-text threshold.

resolutions.decision: Inter — variable font, self-hosted on R2, WOFF2 only, latin + latin-ext subset, under 50KB total budget, font-display: swap. Fallback stack: Inter, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, sans-serif. Body: Inter 400, 16px, line-height 1.55, tracking -0.011em. Display (48px+): Inter 300 for hero sentence, Inter 500 for emphasis, line-height 1.10, tracking -0.022em. UI labels: Inter 600. Analytics figures: font-feature-settings 'tnum'. No secondary typeface. The Q logomark is the only decoration.
resolutions.winning_argument: Selin's battle-tested engineering argument wins: Inter's ClearType hinting on Windows is grade-A and measured at body sizes. The actual user — a Turkish restaurant owner on a six-year-old Windows laptop at midnight — is not the Vercel engineer that Geist signals to. Kaan's Geist argument was audience-captured thinking. Neue Haas Grotesk Display is a licensing trap for an open-source self-hostable product — forks and self-hosters cannot inherit a Monotype license. Selin's exact tracking values (-0.011em body / -0.022em headings) are verified against WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing and are production-ready. Self-hosting on R2 resolves both the Google Fonts privacy footgun and FOUT risk, and is architecturally consistent with the product's own value proposition.
resolutions.dissent: Kaan warned that Inter is 'the lowest-risk way to look expensive' — a contradiction, because low risk and looking expensive are opposites in brand. The guardrail: apply the tracking and line-height specifications with rigor. At display sizes with -0.022em tracking and 1.10 line-height, Inter 300 reads as a considered object, not a default SaaS. The typographic discipline IS the brand signal — the specific typeface is less important than the precision of its application. If Geist Sans MIT-licensed variable WOFF2 can be subsetted under 38KB with equivalent Windows hinting verification, it earns reconsideration at v2.

resolutions.decision: Easing: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) for entrances at 220ms. Exit: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1) at 140ms. Exit faster than entrance — iOS HIG doctrine. Micro-interactions (hover, button press): 200ms entrance, 140ms exit. No bounce easing anywhere. No parallax. No animation above 380ms. prefers-reduced-motion: ALL CSS transforms and transitions collapse to instant (0ms) via @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) wrapping all keyframe and transition blocks. One documented exception: opacity 0-to-1 at 80ms for non-vestibular soft arrival — this is a named token 'opacity-minimal-exception', subject to explicit team approval before any new usage. This exception is not a general policy.
resolutions.winning_argument: Selin's architecture wins: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) as the enabling condition means motion is opt-in at the OS level, not opt-out. This is the unambiguous engineering contract. Kaan's 'never strip all motion — strip vestibular triggers' position, while philosophically defensible, fails in practice: it requires a runtime judgement call about which motion is vestibular under deadline, which is how accessibility debt accumulates. The 80ms opacity exception is a narrow, named, documented carve-out — not Kaan's general principle. Mira's Expo Out curve (cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1)) is adopted for entrances. Selin's faster-exit rule (140ms cubic-bezier(0.4,0,1,1)) is adopted — things leave faster than they arrive. The QR preview updates instantly on keystroke; the typing IS the animation.
resolutions.dissent: Kaan argued that stripping all motion strips life — that opacity is not a vestibular trigger and 150ms opacity transitions are safe. The guardrail: the named 80ms opacity exception in the design system preserves this instinct in constrained form. Any new usage of opacity animation under prefers-reduced-motion must be added to the named exception list with a comment explaining why it is not vestibular. The bar is high. Kaan's staggered QR module 'printing' reveal (8ms row delay, 280ms total) is beautiful and may be revisited if vestibular safety can be clinically documented — it does not ship until that bar is cleared.

resolutions.decision: Dark mode is first-class from day one, designed simultaneously with light mode — same component, different token values, same pixel-level QA. Token schema implemented as CSS custom properties on :root, values set via [data-theme] attribute with @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) as system default. Zero hardcoded hex values in component code — token violations are build-time errors. ABSOLUTE RULE: QR preview card carries explicit color-scheme: light and forced white background regardless of UI theme. Dark modules on white always, minimum 15:1 measured contrast for scannability. Pure black #000000 is banned.
resolutions.winning_argument: All four specialists agreed. Retrofitting dark mode is 5x the technical debt our own rules prohibit. The target user — small business owner printing QR codes at midnight — is in dark mode. The token architecture makes both themes free from day one. Selin's QR-specific override — forcing color-scheme: light on the QR preview card — is the single most important dark mode decision: dark-inverted QR modules tank scan reliability, which is a direct contradiction of the core value proposition 'the QR code that never breaks.' This one forced exception is justified by physical necessity, not aesthetic preference, and must be documented in code comments explaining why. Kaan's process constraint is adopted: simultaneous design in the same component file, not ported after the fact, because light-first design produces wrong elevation logic in dark mode.
resolutions.dissent: No meaningful dissent on day-one dark mode — consensus was complete. The guardrail is operational: any component that ships with a hardcoded hex value is a broken component by definition. The QR white-background override must carry a mandatory code comment explaining the scannability rationale, so future contributors do not 'fix' it as a theme inconsistency.

resolutions.decision: North star: Every token, every interaction, every pixel earns the word reliable. This is the decision filter for every future design argument. 'Permanence made tangible' (Kaan) is the emotional target. 'Effortless trust — the fastest way to a QR you can rely on forever' (Deniz) is the value proposition sentence for marketing. These three statements are complementary: the north star is the test, the emotional target is the direction, the value prop is the tagline. In design review, the test is: does this element earn the word reliable? If the answer requires more than one sentence, the element is removed.
resolutions.winning_argument: Selin's north star is an engineering constraint disguised as design direction — it terminates arguments without a meeting. 'Does this earn the word reliable?' is a binary filter that maps directly to the product promise 'the QR code that never breaks.' Kaan's 'permanence made tangible' tells you what to pursue — durability, solidity, trust. Selin's 'reliable' tells you how to test whether you got there. Deniz's 'effortless trust' tells the market what they receive. These are three altitudes of the same truth. The single word 'reliable' wins as the design north star because it is both a brand promise and a systems requirement simultaneously.
resolutions.dissent: Deniz warned that a beautiful screen that does not get clicked is garbage — that function ranks first and 'calm-but-alive' is texture, not direction. The guardrail: 'reliable' includes reliable conversion. A design that earns the word reliable must also reliably move users from first visit to first QR in under 3 seconds. If the north star is ever used to justify passive beauty over conversion friction, Deniz's warning applies: effortless trust means effortless, not just trustworthy.

color.notes: Pure black #000000 is banned. --color-qr-module and --color-qr-background are invariant across themes — the QR preview card carries an explicit color-scheme: light override. --color-accent is identical in both modes: verified 4.63:1 on #FFFFFF, 4.19:1 on #0D0D0F. No second accent exists in this system. Success, warning, and error states use opacity and lightness shifts of --color-accent, never new hues.

typography.loading: Self-hosted WOFF2 on R2, latin + latin-ext subset only, font-display: swap, total budget under 50KB, variable font axes: wght 300-600 only

body.usage: All body copy, form labels, descriptions

numeric.usage: All analytics figures, scan counts, dates in tables

typography.fallback-stack: Inter, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

design_tokens.spacing: 8px base grid. Scale: 4px (micro-only, borders/gaps), 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px, 32px, 48px, 64px, 96px, 128px. 4px used exclusively for internal component micro-adjustments — never for layout. Component padding minimum: 16px. Touch targets minimum: 44x44px (WCAG 2.5.5 AAA). Hero section vertical padding: 96px top, 64px bottom. Section spacing: 96px between major sections on desktop, 64px on mobile.

radius.notes: QR preview card: --radius-lg (12px). Primary CTA button: --radius-md (8px). Input fields: --radius-md (8px). Badges and chips: --radius-full. Avatar: --radius-full. Modal/sheet: --radius-xl (16px) top corners only on mobile.

shadow.dark-mode-note: Dark mode shadows use same values — the near-black surface (#0D0D0F) absorbs shadow naturally. Do not increase opacity in dark mode.
shadow.usage: QR preview card resting: --shadow-md. QR preview card hover: --shadow-qr-hover at 200ms. Dropdown menus: --shadow-lg. Modal: --shadow-xl. Buttons do not carry a shadow resting state — only on focus ring.

component_principles: Live generator is the hero: the URL input and QR preview are the primary hero composition, not decorations around a headline. The generator works before signup. The QR updates in real time on keystroke. The input is labeled 'Your URL', has focus on desktop load, and carries role=form with aria-label. The QR preview region carries aria-live=polite with a meaningful updating accessible name. The CTA appears only after the user has typed something and reads 'Make it permanent' — never 'Generate'.

QR scannability is non-negotiable and overrides theme: the QR preview card always renders dark modules (#0D0D0F) on a white background (#FFFFFF) regardless of UI theme. The card carries an explicit color-scheme: light CSS property and a forced white background. This is the one intentional user-preference override in the system and must carry a mandatory code comment: /* QR scannability absolute: dark modules on white always — do not remove for theme consistency. See design-system docs §QR-contrast. */ Minimum measured module-to-background contrast: 15:1.

One accent, one viewport: --color-accent (#0A7EA4) appears exactly once in any given viewport — on the single highest-priority interactive element. If two elements compete for accent treatment, one is deprioritized or removed. The accent is never applied to body text, decorative elements, or background fills. On buttons: background --color-accent, label --color-accent-text (#FFFFFF). Focus ring: outline 2px solid var(--color-accent), outline-offset 3px, on every interactive element with zero aesthetic overrides.

Token-first, zero raw hex: every color value in every component file references a CSS custom property. No hardcoded hex values in component code. A component with a raw hex value is a broken component — this is enforced as a build-time lint error, not a code review comment. Dark mode, theming, and future accent migration are free because the token layer is the only source of truth.
accessibility_rules: QR module contrast minimum 15:1 (dark #0D0D0F on white #FFFFFF, measured). QR preview card forces color-scheme: light and explicit white background in all UI themes. This is not optional and not a fast-follow. QR modules are never colorized with the brand accent or any other tint — dark on white, always.

Every interactive element carries a visible focus indicator at all times: outline: 2px solid var(--color-accent); outline-offset: 3px. No aesthetic overrides are permitted. Minimum touch target 44x44px on all interactive elements (WCAG 2.5.5 AAA) — applies to QR download button, copy link, form controls, and navigation items.

All motion is opt-in at the OS level. Every CSS transition, animation, and keyframe block is wrapped in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference). Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, the product delivers instant state changes with one named exception: opacity 0-to-1 at 80ms for non-vestibular soft arrival. This exception is a named design system token ('opacity-minimal-exception') and requires explicit team approval before any new usage. The product must feel completely designed with zero transitions — if it feels dead without motion, the architecture is wrong.

WCAG 1.4.3 contrast compliance is a shipping gate, not a post-ship audit. --color-accent (#0A7EA4) is verified at 4.63:1 on #FFFFFF and 4.19:1 on #0D0D0F before any component ships. --color-text-primary achieves 15:1+ on --color-surface-0 in both themes. --color-text-secondary achieves 4.5:1+ on --color-surface-0 in both themes. Any new color token must include measured contrast ratios in its definition comment. The live QR generator must be fully operable by keyboard alone and by screen reader: role=form on the generator, aria-label, aria-live=polite on the QR preview region with a meaningful updating description, complete Tab sequence from input to QR download with no modal traps.

motion_system.enter_easing_name: Expo Out — fast attack, long organic tail, no bounce
motion_system.exit_easing_name: Ease In — things leave faster than they arrive (iOS HIG doctrine)

durations.micro: 200ms enter / 140ms exit — hover states, button press, input focus ring
durations.reveal: 350ms enter / 140ms exit — card appearance, QR preview first render, dropdown open
durations.qr_update: instant module render on keystroke — the typing IS the animation, no transition on QR modules themselves

motion_system.hover_qr_hero: transform: scale(1.02) at 200ms cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1); box-shadow transitions from --shadow-md to --shadow-qr-hover at same duration. On pointer leave: scale(1.0) and shadow revert at 140ms cubic-bezier(0.4,0,1,1).
motion_system.button_press: transform: translateY(1px) at 80ms linear on :active. Revert at 140ms cubic-bezier(0.4,0,1,1).
motion_system.max_duration: 380ms — any animation above this threshold is perceived as lag by 2026 users, not as luxury.
no_go_list: Bounce easing anywhere in the product
Staggered QR module 'printing' reveal (vestibular risk, does not ship without clinical documentation)
Spring overshoot on any functional element

reduced_motion.implementation: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { /* all keyframes and transitions go here */ }
reduced_motion.behavior_under_reduce: Instant state changes — 0ms transitions on all transforms, scales, and layout properties. One named exception: opacity 0-to-1 at 80ms only, using the design system token 'opacity-minimal-exception'. This exception list is fixed and requires explicit team approval to extend.
reduced_motion.philosophy: Motion is opt-in at the OS level. If the product feels lifeless without motion, the architecture is over-reliant on motion — that is a design problem, not a motion problem. The product must be complete and feel considered with zero transitions.
reduced_motion.css_variable_approach: Define --duration-enter: 220ms and --duration-exit: 140ms as custom properties. Under reduced-motion media query, reassign: --duration-enter: 0ms; --duration-exit: 0ms; --duration-opacity: 80ms only for the named exception.
